title: Recent Inflation Developments and Challenges for Research and Monetary Policymaking
summary: Loretta Mester, then President of the Cleveland Fed, delivered a speech at the Konstanz Seminar in May 2016 reviewing recent inflation developments across the U.S., UK, and Euro area, where inflation had run persistently below central bank targets. The speech discusses the Fed's 2% PCE inflation target (established January 2012) and attributes low inflation to weak global demand, declining energy/commodity prices, and dollar appreciation. Mester emphasizes the ongoing challenges of accurately measuring, forecasting, and understanding inflation determinants for monetary policy.
key_points: The Fed formally adopted its 2% PCE inflation target in January 2012, viewed as symmetric (concern warranted if persistently above or below target)
In 2015, inflation was 0.66% in the U.S. (PCE), 0.20% in the U.K. (CPI), and 0.25% in the Euro area (HICP) — all well below respective targets
Common factors driving low inflation: post-financial crisis weak demand, energy/commodity price decline, and dollar appreciation
Fed staff SIGMA model simulation: a 10% real dollar appreciation reduces core inflation by ~0.5% after one year via import prices
Mester explicitly notes these are her own views, not necessarily those of the FOMC or Federal Reserve System
Speech emphasizes that achieving price stability requires measuring inflation, forecasting it, understanding transmission mechanisms, and operating under uncertainty
why_it_matters: This speech documents the inflation environment and policy thinking from mid-2016, a period when major central banks were grappling with persistently below-target inflation. The analysis of dollar appreciation's effect on import prices and the model-based estimates provide useful historical context for understanding how the Fed interpreted inflation dynamics in the post-crisis period.
macro_context: The speech contextualizes the post-Great Recession low inflation environment across advanced economies. Key macro insight: dollar appreciation exerts meaningful downward pressure on core inflation (0.5% effect per 10% appreciation) with a lag. The speech also references the Volcker era disinflation as historical precedent for the costs of losing focus on price stability.
important_numbers: 0.5% — estimated core inflation decline from a 10% real dollar appreciation after one year (SIGMA model)
